query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid method that combines high-throughput DSC measurements with CALPHAD modeling can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and selected liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy alloy family.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) produced in an as-cast, near-equiatomic state with complex multi-element compositions.
generation.intervention: Implement high-throughput DSC experiments up to and beyond the solidus temperature alongside CALPHAD modeling calibrated against binary and ternary subsystems to predict the complete fusion thermodynamics and liquid-phase behavior.
generation.conditions: Measurements and simulations conducted under controlled laboratory conditions. DSC runs must cover temperature ranges from room temperature up to and past the melting region, while CALPHAD models are updated with available thermodynamic data for constituent binary/ternary interactions.
generation.structural_mediator: The configurational entropy inherent to HEAs mediates the link between atomic-scale mixing effects and observed macroscopic phase transition behaviors, which is captured both by the experimental DSC data and the CALPHAD predictions.
generation.mechanism: DSC provides reliable, direct measurements of heat flow, capturing the rapid increase in heat capacity at the solidus and melting events, while CALPHAD modeling leverages known thermodynamic data to estimate property trends across a wide compositional space. Their combination helps mitigate individual uncertainties by using DSC data to validate and recalibrate the computational predictions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid approach is expected to yield estimates of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting with an accuracy on the order of ±10–15% compared to results from exhaustive, conventional experiments. Trend predictions (e.g., melting temperature depressions due to configurational entropy effects) will be captured reliably across the HEA compositional range.
generation.baseline: Standalone DSC measurements on multi-component HEAs often involve considerable uncertainty due to complex phase behavior, while CALPHAD modeling in isolation may fail when databases are incomplete; both limitations are reduced in the hybrid approach.
generation.boundary: This approach is primarily applicable to HEA systems where sufficient thermodynamic assessment of at least the relevant binary and ternary subsystems exists. Its effectiveness may be limited for alloy compositions with poorly characterized interactions or when experimental DSC resolution is compromised.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative performance hinges on the quality of DSC calibration and on the completeness of the CALPHAD databases for multi-component interactions. In some HEA systems, the precise error margins are uncertain and may vary, particularly where data on ternary/quaternary interactions are scarce.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of high-entropy alloys with well-documented binary and ternary interaction data. Perform high-throughput DSC experiments to capture melting behavior (melting temperature, ΔH and ΔS of fusion, and volume change using complementary dilatometry or density measurements). Independently generate CALPHAD predictions for these same alloys. Statistically compare the experimental values to the predictions.
measurements: DSC thermograms to extract melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion
Volume change at melting measured via dilatometry or density assessments
CALPHAD-modeled thermodynamic properties for the same alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, for the majority of alloys tested, the discrepancies between DSC-based measurements and CALPHAD predictions exceed ±15% consistently, or if the hybrid approach fails to capture the expected trends (e.g., melting temperature depressions due to configurational entropy effects) across the compositional space, then the proposed method would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The Gibbs free energy, G=H−TS, is the established thermodynamic criterion for phase selection, where H is enthalpy, S is entropy and T is absolute temperature. The Gibbs free energies for SS phases are described by enthalpies and entropies of mixing (Hmix and Smix), and IM phases are characterized by enthalpies and entropies of formation (Hf and Sf). The Gibbs free energies for all competing phases must be estimated, and the phase (or phases) with the lowest G gives the stable microstructure for that alloy. Smix, also called configurational entropy, is easy to modeland Hmix has been estimated for wide range of atom pairs. Sf for IM compounds is generally very small, and is often estimated to be zero. Hf of IM compounds is an essential term, but is difficult to estimate—there are no general models. Hmix is sometimes used as a proxy for Hf, but the differences between these values can be very large, and at best this approach gives only a relative ranking that cannot be used to determine G. Fundamental approaches to calculate Hf are available but are difficult to apply to over 100,000 alloys as in the present case. To overcome these barriers, here we use the CALPHAD approach to perfor

The Calphad approach is used widely in the high entropy alloys and ceramics field [,,]. Senkov et al. demonstrated [] that for high entropy alloys, Calphad computations of type and number of phases agreed well with experimental results only when more than half of binary systems were fully assessed; however, even when there are enough data on binary and ternary systems, Calphad predictions of transformation temperatures, phase compositions and fractions are challenging. Compared with metals, the databases for oxides are much more limited, especially for the temperature range addressed in this study. Nevertheless, it is instructive to compare our experimental results with Calphad predictions.

The effects of cold rolling on the phase transformation kinetics of an Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy are studied by the thermal expansion method. The transformed volume fraction–temperature curves of as-cast and 20% cold rolling Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys are determined by the lever rule method using thermal expansion curves. Using the KAS method, the mean activation energy for as-cast and deformed HEAs calculated are 181 kJ/mol and 159 kJ/mol, respectively. The kinetic exponent is determined using the local Avrami exponent method based on the JMA equation. Both as-cast and deformed samples show the three stages of kinetic exponent variations, and the deformed alloy shows a much larger value compared with the as-cast alloy, indicating a much higher nucleation and growth rate. The reason for the kinetic exponent variations are thought to be related with the deformation induced strain and defects inside the sample that can generate a much higher energy that favors the nucleation and growth process.

reading.lever: Combine high-throughput DSC measurements with CALPHAD modeling to efficiently and accurately predict melting properties across HEAs.
reading.why: This combination leverages the experimental reliability of DSC for validation with the computational efficiency of CALPHAD for broad compositional coverage.
